tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000 for a foreground command.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SearchPlugins
tools.description:
Search the user's claude.ai plugin catalog by keyword. Call this when a plugin (slash command, skill bundle, hook, or agent) from the user's org catalog might help complete the task. The user does not need to name a plugin: search when the task depends on their team's own process, systems or data and nothing you already have, the project's own scripts included, covers it.

Examples:
- "use the deploy plugin" → keywords ["deploy"]
- "is there something for linting?" → keywords ["lint", "format", "code quality"]
- "ship this to staging" → keywords ["deploy", "release", "staging"]
- "review this contract against our playbook" → keywords ["legal", "contract", "playbook"]
- "which deals close this week?" → keywords ["sales", "pipeline", "crm"]

Do not search unasked for one-off questions or tasks you can handle directly ("explain this regex", "fix this typo"), or after the user ignored a suggestion in this conversation.

Returns a ranked list with id, name, description, and whether the plugin is already enabled for this session (in a channel session, whether the channel has it). When results fit and SuggestPluginInstall is among your tools, call it to render the install card; otherwise relay the relevant results in text instead. If nothing relevant, proceed without mentioning that you searched.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

caption.description: Optional short caption for the file(s).

status.description: Use 'proactive' when you're surfacing a file the user hasn't asked for and needs to see now — a generated artifact, a completed report. Use 'normal' when replying to something the user just said.

display.description: How the client should present the file. 'render' opens it inline in the side panel (for HTML, SVG, Mermaid, images, PDFs — anything the user wants to look at now). 'attach' shows a download card only, no inline preview (for deliverables the user will save and open elsewhere). Omit to let the client decide by file type — today that means renderable types render and everything else attaches, same as before this parameter existed.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

prompt.description: The initial message for the spawned session. Self-contained — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation. Not shown directly in the UI.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

Use this whenever the user wants to see or try their iOS app — "run my app", "test this on iPhone", "does this look right?", "try the new screen" — not only when they mention the simulator by name. action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

content.content:
1	# Git workflow — CS 370 HW1
2	
3	Kept outside the repo on purpose: this is a personal reference, not a
4	deliverable. The repo stays clean for the clean-clone check before submission.
5	
6	Repo lives at:
7	`Homeworks/hw1/Github Repo CS370 HW1/CS370---HW1---Red-Black-Tree-in-C/`
8	
9	---
10	
11	## Vocabulary
12	
13	- **green** — everything passed
14	- **red** — something failed
15	- **staged** — marked to go into the next commit (`git add` does this)
16	- **working tree** — the files as they currently are on disk
17	- **commit** — a saved snapshot in your local history
18	- **push** — upload commits to GitHub. Nothing is backed up until you push.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## The loop
23	
24	Run this cycle every time you finish a slice of work.
25	
26	### 1. Pull (start of session)
27	```
28	git pull
29	```
30	`Already up to date.` is the normal answer when working solo on one machine.
31	Matters if you edit on GitHub's website or start using a Linux box.
32	
33	### 2. Edit
34	The actual work.
35	
36	### 3. Get green
37	```
38	make test && make asan
39	```
40	`&&` means asan only runs if test passed. Red means you are still working,
41	not committing.
42	
43	**Expect the test output to appear TWICE.** `make asan` is defined as
44	`asan: clean test` — it wipes `build/`, recompiles with sanitizer flags, and
45	re-runs the same tests. Two "passed" lines is success. One means something
46	stopped early. The `rm -rf build` and the `-fsanitize=...` gcc lines separate
47	the two runs.
48	
49	### 4. See what changed
50	```
51	git status
52	```
53	Red = changed, not staged. Green = staged, ready to commit.
54	
55	### 5. Read the diff — do not skip
56	```
57	git diff
58	```
59	Better in VS Code: Source Control panel (branch icon in the sidebar, or
60	Ctrl+Shift+G), click a file for side-by-side view.
61	
62	Read test file diffs especially. The known failure mode of coding agents is
63	quietly weakening a test until it passes — a loosened assertion, a deleted
64	case, a threshold drifting down. Your eyes here are the only thing that

# Git workflow — CS 370 HW1

Kept outside the repo on purpose: this is a personal reference, not a
deliverable. The repo stays clean for the clean-clone check before submission.

Repo lives at:
`Homeworks/hw1/Github Repo CS370 HW1/CS370---HW1---Red-Black-Tree-in-C/`

---

## Vocabulary

- **green** — everything passed
- **red** — something failed
- **staged** — marked to go into the next commit (`git add` does this)
- **working tree** — the files as they currently are on disk
- **commit** — a saved snapshot in your local history
- **push** — upload commits to GitHub. Nothing is backed up until you push.

---

## The loop

Run this cycle every time you finish a slice of work.

### 1. Pull (start of session)
```
git pull
```
`Already up to date.` is the normal answer when working solo on one machine.
Matters if you edit on GitHub's website or start using a Linux box.

### 2. Edit
The actual work.

### 3. Get green
```
make test && make asan
```
`&&` means asan only runs if test passed. Red means you are still working,
not committing.

**Expect the test output to appear TWICE.** `make asan` is defined as
`asan: clean test` — it wipes `build/`, recompiles with sanitizer flags, and
re-runs the same tests. Two "passed" lines is success. One means something
stopped early. The `rm -rf build` and the `-fsanitize=...` gcc lines separate
the two runs.

### 4. See what changed
```
git status
```
Red = changed, not staged. Green = staged, ready to commit.

### 5. Read the diff — do not skip
```
git diff
```
Better in VS Code: Source Control panel (branch icon in the sidebar, or
Ctrl+Shift+G), click a file for side-by-side view.

Read test file diffs especially. The known failure mode of coding agents is
quietly weakening a test until it passes — a loosened assertion, a deleted
case, a threshold drifting down. Your eyes here are the only thing that
catches it.

### 6. Stage
```
git add -A
```
Or selectively: `git add src/rbtree.c tests/test_rbtree.c`

### 7. Commit
```
git commit -m "M1: rotations, with t->root updated inside rotate_left/right"
```
Format is set in CLAUDE.md: `M<n>: <what>`. Say what changed and why.
A grader reads these against your session transcripts.

For a longer message, run `git commit` with no `-m` — an editor opens.
First line is the summary, then a blank line, then the body.

### 8. Push
```
git push
```

---

## Why `git diff` sometimes shows nothing

Two different causes:

| Situation                   | `git diff` | `git status` shows     |
|-----------------------------|------------|------------------------|
| Nothing changed at all      | empty      | no files               |
| Changed, then `git add`ed   | empty      | the file, in green     |

In the second case use `git diff --staged`. `git diff` compares the working
tree against the staging area, and after staging they match.

---

## Command reference

| Command                       | What it does                                  |
|-------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------|
| `git status`                  | What changed, what's staged, how far ahead     |
| `git diff`                    | Unstaged changes                               |
| `git diff --staged`           | Staged changes                                 |
| `git log --oneline`           | History, one line per commit                   |
| `git show <hash>`             | Everything one commit changed                  |
| `git add -A`                  | Stage everything                               |
| `git add <file>`              | Stage one file                                 |
| `git restore <file>`          | THROW AWAY uncommitted changes to a file       |
| `git restore .`               | Throw away all uncommitted changes             |
| `git restore --staged <file>` | Unstage, keep the edits                        |
| `git commit -m "..."`         | Commit staged changes                          |
| `git push`                    | Upload to GitHub                               |
| `git pull`                    | Download from GitHub                           |

**`git restore` is the escape hatch.** When a debugging session has made the
code worse than when you started: instant, free, back to your last commit.
Which is also the argument for committing often — restore can only take you
back as far as your last commit.

---

## Commit cadence

The spec requires **8 or more meaningful commits**. A single "final
submission" commit is an automatic zero on the process grade.

Rule of thumb: **if `make test` just went green and you'd be annoyed to lose
the work, commit.** That lands you around 12-15 naturally.

Commit ≠ push ≠ milestone:
- **commit** — every green state, several per evening. This is what's graded.
- **push** — backup. End of session is plenty. Not graded.
- **milestone** — M0-M3. A grading unit containing many commits.

---

## Working alongside Claude

Claude edits the same files on disk that VS Code has open — it does not drive
the VS Code UI. **Save in VS Code (Cmd+S) before asking Claude to edit a
file**, or the editor buffer and the disk will disagree and whoever saves
last wins.

Claude does not run `git commit` or `git push` — those are yours.

1	# HW1 Spec Notes — "Building Your First Red-Black Tree in C"
2	
3	**Source:** `CS370-HW1.pdf` (kept in this folder, not deleted — original stays as reference)
4	**Version:** 1.0, released 2026-08-25 · **Points:** 5 total
5	**One-line description:** Implement a red-black tree in C behind a frozen header, with airtight
6	memory management (verified by ASan/UBSan + valgrind), using Claude Code as a required,
7	disciplined collaborator — not a solve-it-for-me tool.
8	
9	This is note #1 of 2 for this assignment. See [howto-notes.md](howto-notes.md) for the companion
10	walkthrough (the "how to work" document). This file covers the graded spec itself: what to build,
11	what's frozen, how it's graded, and the AI-usage rules that are actually enforced.
12	
13	## The big picture / why this assignment is shaped this way
14	
15	- This is **half of a two-assignment pair**. The tree built here gets reused, unmodified in spirit,
16	  in the *next* assignment — which adds custom allocators, injected allocation failures, and
17	  stack-limited (non-recursive) teardown. A near-twin of this tree later becomes part of the
18	  CPU scheduler in Assignment 4 (Linux's CFS runqueue uses a real red-black tree). **Nothing built
19	  here is throwaway** — build it to be understood, not just passed.
20	- Two intertwined goals: (1) a **systems goal** — correct, leak-free, double-free-free C — and
21	  (2) a **process-engineering-with-AI goal** — learn to direct Claude Code like a senior engineer
22	  directs a capable-but-overconfident junior.
23	- Explicit anti-goal: pasting the spec into Claude and saying "solve this." This actively hurts the
24	  grade (see Grading below) because of the process/transcript component and the live walkthrough.
25	
26	## What is a Red-Black Tree (the actual CS content)
27	
28	Five rules:
29	1. Every node is red or black.
30	2. The root is black.
31	3. Every missing child is conceptually a black sentinel leaf, `NIL`.
32	4. A red node has only black children (no two reds in a row on any path).
33	5. Every root-to-NIL path has the same number of black nodes = the **black-height**.
34	
35	Consequence: height h ≤ 2·log₂(n+1), so search/insert/delete are all O(log n) worst case.
36	
37	**Insertion** — new node always inserted **red** (keeps black-height unchanged everywhere; the only
38	possible damage is a red-red edge = a *local*, addressable violation).
39	- Fixup loop, red-uncle case: uncle is red → recolor parent+uncle black, grandparent red, then
40	  recheck two levels up. **No pointers move.** This can repeat — the violation just relocates
41	  upward; it is NOT guaranteed to finish in one pass.
42	- Key fact: **on the very first iteration of the fixup loop, a black uncle is always NIL** (a real
43	  black-with-subtrees uncle literally cannot occur yet — proven by a black-height counting
44	  argument). Rotation cases with substantial uncles only show up after the loop has already
45	  climbed once — meaning hand-testing with 5 keys will never exercise them; you need real
46	  volume (fuzzing) to hit rotation cases.
47	- When uncle is black: recoloring can't help. Need 1–2 rotations (zig-zag "kink" needs 2: one to
48	  straighten the shape, one to do the real repair + color swap). **Insert fixup never needs more
49	  than 2 rotations, total.**
50	- **Classic bug:** after a rotation moves the root to a new node, if your fixup only patches
51	  parent/child pointers and never updates `t->root`, `rb_find` starts silently searching a subtree
52	  and `rb_validate` will happily certify the (wrong) subtree as legal. Write a **stale-root
53	  regression test** the same day you write rotations.
54	
55	**Deletion** — the unpleasant direction; damage is a *global count mismatch*, not a local violation.
56	- Removing a **red leaf** is free (no invariant impact).
57	- A node with **two children**: hoist the in-order successor's key+value into the doomed node's
58	  slot, then delete the successor instead (which has ≤1 child by construction). "Hoist" = transfer
59	  *ownership* of the key allocation — get this wrong and you get two nodes both believing they own
60	  the same key (→ double free at `rb_destroy` time).
61	- Every deletion funnels down to: **what happens when the physically unlinked node is black?**
62	  → creates a "doubly black" deficit — an **accounting fiction**, not a third color in the enum.
63	  The empty slot "owes" one black; fixup's job is paying that debt off by climbing toward the root.
64	- Deletion fixup case families (mirror images exist for all — don't forget them):
65	  - Sibling is black with no red children → recolor sibling red, debt moves up one level (if
66	    parent absorbs it by being red → turns black, done, no pointers moved — the "cheap" case,
67	    deletion's mirror of the red-uncle insert case).
68	  - Sibling has a red child → rotation drags that red across to the deficient side.
69	  - Sibling itself is red → rotate first just to reach a shape you already know how to handle.
70	  - Debt reaching the root just dissolves there (every path lost the same one black — equality
71	    restored, absolute black-height may drop by one, which is fine).
72	  - **Special/easy corner case:** deleting a black node with exactly one child. That child is
73	    *provably* red (proof by counting — a black child there would already have broken the tree
74	    before you touched it). Fix: splice the red child into the vacant slot, paint it black. Done —
75	    no debt, no fixup loop at all. **If your code launches the full sibling case analysis here,
76	    something is wrong** — this must be tested explicitly (spec calls out adding this exact case
77	    to the required table-driven tests).
78	- **Memory-safety tripwire repeated multiple times in the spec:** fixup must NEVER dereference
79	  freed memory. Either save everything you need (parent/sibling/slot info) *before* calling
80	  `free()` on the removed node, or restructure to free *after* fixup completes. Either order is
81	  fine; the ordering violation is not.
82	
83	## From Java to C (field guide) — the two questions that matter for every pointer
84	
85	For every pointer-like thing in this assignment, ask: **(1) how long does the pointee live, and
86	(2) who is responsible for eventually freeing it?** Java answered both silently; C answers neither.
87	
88	- Pointer ≠ object. Copying a pointer copies an address, not the thing at that address (aliasing
89	  works like Java references — two names, one object — but *ownership* is a separate concept from
90	  *reachability*: many pointers can reach an object; exactly one owns it).
91	- `malloc(n)` gives raw, uninitialized, unconstructed bytes — nothing more. `free(p)` exactly once,
92	  never touch that pointer again after.
93	- Named failure modes: **leak** (never freed), **double free** (freed twice — corrupts allocator
94	  bookkeeping), **use-after-free** (freed then still used — "the most treacherous," because it
95	  often *keeps working* for a while).
96	- Local/stack variables die when their function returns — anything that must outlive the call
97	  (every tree node, every private key copy) needs heap storage via `malloc`.
98	- `malloc` **can return NULL** — must check every allocation. Partial-failure cleanup matters: if
99	  node alloc succeeds but the subsequent key-copy alloc fails, the first allocation is still yours
100	  to free ("the second malloc failed" is not an exemption from cleaning up the first).
101	- C strings are `char*` arrays terminated by `'\0'`. `==` on two strings compares **addresses**, not
102	  contents (bug you'll write once, remember forever) — use `strcmp(a,b) == 0`. Copying a string
103	  means `malloc(strlen(s) + 1)` — **never forget the +1** for the terminator.
104	- One logical tree node = **two separate heap allocations** (the node struct itself, and its private
105	  heap copy of the key string) — both must be tracked and freed, not just one.
106	- `struct` = fields only, no methods/constructors — `malloc`ing one gives raw bytes; you initialize
107	  every field yourself. Idiom: `malloc(sizeof *n)` — ties the allocation size to the pointer's type
108	  automatically.
109	- The public header uses an **opaque type** (`typedef struct rbtree rbtree_t;` with no visible
110	  fields) — C's version of "private," enforced by the compiler simply never being told the layout.
111	- A `parent` pointer is optional but common — makes fixup loops easier to write (classic textbook
112	  algorithms assume one), at the cost of one more pointer to keep correct through every rotation.
113	  **This is flagged as "your first real design decision."**
114	
115	## Ownership contract (the actual grading contract — read like a lease)
116	
117	- `rb_insert`: **on success**, the tree takes ownership of `value` (caller must never free it — the
118	  tree will, via `value_free`, when appropriate). **On failure** (`-1`), ownership never transferred
119	  — caller still owns `value` and must handle it. **On overwrite** of an existing key, the tree
120	  frees the *old* value before installing the new one (tree is the old value's only owner at that
121	  moment).
122	- Track three things separately per node: the node allocation, the tree's private key copy, and the
123	  opaque `value` (whose ownership follows the API rules above — not tied to node/key lifetime).
124	- Rotations change **topology only** — they never change who owns a node/key/value.
125	
126	## Frozen API (`include/rbtree.h`) — NEVER MODIFY
127	
128	```c
129	rbtree_t *rb_create(rb_value_free_fn value_free);      // NULL on alloc failure; value_free may be NULL
130	int       rb_insert(rbtree_t *t, const char *key, void *value); // 0 ok, -1 on alloc failure (unchanged, value NOT consumed)
131	void     *rb_find(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key);          // tree retains ownership
132	int       rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key);              // 0 ok, -1 if absent; frees key copy + value
133	size_t    rb_size(const rbtree_t *t);
134	void      rb_foreach(const rbtree_t *t, void (*fn)(const char*, void*, void*), void *ctx); // in-order
135	int       rb_validate(const rbtree_t *t);                       // 0 iff all invariants hold
136	void      rb_destroy(rbtree_t *t);                               // frees everything, NULL-safe
137	```
138	Keys are C strings, copied and owned by the tree. Values are opaque `void *`.
139	
140	## Milestones (M0–M3 + optional Reach)
141	
142	| Milestone | What | Est. hours |
143	|---|---|---|
144	| M0 | Setup: repo, `CLAUDE.md`, toolchain | 1 |
145	| M1 | Skeleton, insert (+rebalance), find, foreach, validate | 3–4 |
146	| M2 | Delete (all fixup cases) + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops), green under asan+memcheck | 3–4 |
147	| M3 | Hardening, edge cases, final clean sweep | 1–2 |
148	| The Reach (ungraded) | Teardown *without recursion* — O(1) aux space via right-spine trick | 1–2 |
149	| — | Process artifacts (CLAUDE.md, PROMPTLOG.md, REFLECTION.md), written throughout | 1 |
150	
151	**Discipline point emphasized repeatedly:** don't debug delete on top of an insert you don't trust
152	yet — "less a milestone than an archaeological dig."
153	
154	### Required operations & testing bar
155	- Required: `rb_create`, `rb_insert` (w/ rebalancing), `rb_find`, `rb_delete` (full fixup, all
156	  cases), `rb_size`, `rb_foreach` (in-order), `rb_validate`, `rb_destroy`.
157	- `rb_validate` must check all 5 invariants + that `rb_size` matches actual node count.
158	- **Fuzzer:** ≥ 10⁵ random insert/find/delete ops vs. a reference model (sorted array or linked
159	  list is fine), calling `rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, under both asan and memcheck.
160	- **Targeted deletion tests are required in addition to fuzzing** (fuzzing alone won't reliably hit
161	  rare fixup shapes): minimum a red leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a two-children node,
162	  root deletion — **plus the black-node-with-one-red-child case** the spec adds explicitly. Each
163	  test must assert `rb_validate` and `rb_size` afterward.
164	- **Recursion is allowed** in `rb_destroy`/`rb_foreach` *for this assignment only* — the next
165	  assignment revokes it (stack-limited kernel-style constraints).
166	- **Tip explicitly recommended:** route all allocation through 4-line wrapper functions
167	  `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` (just forwarding to malloc/free for now) — this is the "seam" the *next*
168	  assignment's fault-injection harness will need. Install now, "while the house is small."
169	
170	## Toolchain / verification requirements
171	
172	- Must compile clean: `gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`.
173	- `make asan` — AddressSanitizer + UBSan (compiled-in instrumentation; fast, pinpoints the exact
174	  bad instruction).
175	- `make memcheck` — valgrind (external, no rebuild needed, catches some uninitialized-read cases
176	  ASan misses; much slower). Required together — "belt and suspenders," deliberately redundant.
177	- **Hard rule: a single leaked byte, invalid read/write, or UB report caps that milestone's
178	  correctness score at 50%.** Not a warning — a failure, mechanically enforced.
179	
180	## Deliverables (submitted as a tar via Canvas)
181	
182	- Source: Makefile, `src/rbtree.c`, tests, the **unmodified** frozen `include/rbtree.h`.
183	- `CLAUDE.md` — checked in, evolving across milestones.
184	- `PROMPTLOG.md` — **4–6 annotated episodes** (prompt + response + your judgment: accepted /
185	  rejected / pushed back, and why). Must include at minimum: one plan you revised, one
186	  rejected/oversized diff, one tool-output debugging loop, one review finding you triaged.
187	  **Raw transcript dumps score nothing here — annotation is the actual deliverable.**
188	- `REFLECTION.md` (~1 page): where the agent was most/least reliable; one bug it introduced that
189	  you caught and how; what most surprised "the Java programmer you were two weeks ago."
190	- **Raw Claude Code session transcripts** (`.jsonl` files, unmodified, not exported/retyped) —
191	  found locally at `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl`. **These auto-purge after 30
192	  days** — copy them out periodically; losing them is not a valid excuse.
193	- Git history with **≥ 8 meaningful commits** tracking milestones — a single "final submission"
194	  commit is an **automatic process-grade of zero**.
195	
196	## Grading breakdown (5 points total)
197	
198	| Component | Method | Points |
199	|---|---|---|
200	| Core tree (insert/find/foreach/validate) | Unit tests + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops) under asan+memcheck | 1.5 |
201	| Deletion, all fixup cases | Table-driven case tests + fuzzer w/ deletes green | 1.5 |
202	| Code quality & memory cleanliness | Clean build, zero sanitizer/valgrind findings, sane structure | 1.0 |
203	| **Program correctness subtotal** | | **4.0** |
204	| Prompt analysis (transcripts) | TA review for genuine iterative use, corroborated vs. repo | 0.5 |
205	| Quiz (live walkthrough, on your own code) | Short quiz generated from your submitted code | 0.5 |
206	| **Total** | | **5.0** |
207	
208	### Transcript grading is evidence-based, not narrative-based
209	"The grade is based on what can be corroborated against the repository, never on the log's own
210	narrative." A grader (headless Claude) cross-checks claims in the transcript against actual git
211	commits/diffs/tests. **A confident but unverifiable story scores below a modest, checkable one.**
212	5-level scale, 0.1 pts per level: Level 5 = "verified engineering dialogue" (every episode
213	cross-checks against a commit/test/diff) down to Level 1 = "performative or contradicted" (narrative
214	conflicts with git history / episodes appear fabricated).
215	
216	## Rules of engagement for AI use
217	
218	- **Allowed/expected:** explore, plan, implement, test, debug, review with Claude Code; ask it to
219	  explain concepts; have it write test scaffolding/Makefiles.
220	- **Required:** the process deliverables above, raw transcripts, git history with ≥8 commits.
221	- **Forbidden:** submitting code you cannot personally explain. "Claude wrote it" is not an
222	  explanation.
223	- **You own the bugs.** If the agent introduces a use-after-free and you commit it, it's yours to
224	  explain, full stop.
225	
226	## Personalized Verification (live walkthrough) — mandatory for EVERY student
227	
228	Not a flagged-subset spot check — everyone sits for it. You'll be given a small, previously-unseen
229	modification to make live, starting only from your own submitted source (e.g. a new CLI flag, a
230	new key-length range). Plus questions about specific lines of your own code ("why is this node
231	recolored?", "what frees this key copy on the overwrite path?") and a `PROMPTLOG.md` episode you
232	must defend. **This is explicitly why understanding matters more than a working submission alone —
233	a static submission can only prove a plausible-looking result exists, not that you built it.**
234	
235	## Workflow steps required (Section 11 of spec) — summarized (see howto-notes.md for the practical version)
236	
237	1. Give the agent persistent context via `CLAUDE.md` (`/init` then hand-edit — build/test commands,
238	   frozen-header rule, style rules, "smallest change that passes").
239	2. Explore before writing anything (fresh session, questions only, no edits).
240	3. **Plan mode** (Shift+Tab) for every milestone — agent can read/analyze but not edit. Argue with
241	   the plan before approving; a plan accepted unmodified on first try is flagged as a red flag.
242	4. Tests first, then the smallest implementation slice — reject any diff that's too big ("one case
243	   only").
244	5. Close the loop with tool evidence — never accept "should pass now"; feed real tool output back.
245	6. Manage context: `/clear` between milestones, `/compact` mid-task when a debugging thread gets
246	   noisy. Rule of thumb: new milestone → new session.
247	7. **Adversarial review in a fresh context** before each milestone commit (`/code-review` skill or
248	   manually `/clear` + hostile-reviewer prompt) — hunts specifically for use-after-free in successor
249	   splice, leaked key copy on overwrite, unchecked NULL, missed subtrees in `rb_destroy`.
250	8. Git discipline — commit at every green state, conversationally directing the agent to do so
251	   *after you've read the diff*.
252	9. (Optional) Automate the battery as a slash command (`.claude/commands/battery.md`).
253	
254	## Practical logistics

# HW1 Spec Notes — "Building Your First Red-Black Tree in C"

**Source:** `CS370-HW1.pdf` (kept in this folder, not deleted — original stays as reference)
**Version:** 1.0, released 2026-08-25 · **Points:** 5 total
**One-line description:** Implement a red-black tree in C behind a frozen header, with airtight
memory management (verified by ASan/UBSan + valgrind), using Claude Code as a required,
disciplined collaborator — not a solve-it-for-me tool.

This is note #1 of 2 for this assignment. See [howto-notes.md](howto-notes.md) for the companion
walkthrough (the "how to work" document). This file covers the graded spec itself: what to build,
what's frozen, how it's graded, and the AI-usage rules that are actually enforced.

## The big picture / why this assignment is shaped this way

- This is **half of a two-assignment pair**. The tree built here gets reused, unmodified in spirit,
  in the *next* assignment — which adds custom allocators, injected allocation failures, and
  stack-limited (non-recursive) teardown. A near-twin of this tree later becomes part of the
  CPU scheduler in Assignment 4 (Linux's CFS runqueue uses a real red-black tree). **Nothing built
  here is throwaway** — build it to be understood, not just passed.
- Two intertwined goals: (1) a **systems goal** — correct, leak-free, double-free-free C — and
  (2) a **process-engineering-with-AI goal** — learn to direct Claude Code like a senior engineer
  directs a capable-but-overconfident junior.
- Explicit anti-goal: pasting the spec into Claude and saying "solve this." This actively hurts the
  grade (see Grading below) because of the process/transcript component and the live walkthrough.

## What is a Red-Black Tree (the actual CS content)

Five rules:
1. Every node is red or black.
2. The root is black.
3. Every missing child is conceptually a black sentinel leaf, `NIL`.
4. A red node has only black children (no two reds in a row on any path).
5. Every root-to-NIL path has the same number of black nodes = the **black-height**.

Consequence: height h ≤ 2·log₂(n+1), so search/insert/delete are all O(log n) worst case.

**Insertion** — new node always inserted **red** (keeps black-height unchanged everywhere; the only
possible damage is a red-red edge = a *local*, addressable violation).
- Fixup loop, red-uncle case: uncle is red → recolor parent+uncle black, grandparent red, then
  recheck two levels up. **No pointers move.** This can repeat — the violation just relocates
  upward; it is NOT guaranteed to finish in one pass.
- Key fact: **on the very first iteration of the fixup loop, a black uncle is always NIL** (a real
  black-with-subtrees uncle literally cannot occur yet — proven by a black-height counting
  argument). Rotation cases with substantial uncles only show up after the loop has already
  climbed once — meaning hand-testing with 5 keys will never exercise them; you need real
  volume (fuzzing) to hit rotation cases.
- When uncle is black: recoloring can't help. Need 1–2 rotations (zig-zag "kink" needs 2: one to
  straighten the shape, one to do the real repair + color swap). **Insert fixup never needs more
  than 2 rotations, total.**
- **Classic bug:** after a rotation moves the root to a new node, if your fixup only patches
  parent/child pointers and never updates `t->root`, `rb_find` starts silently searching a subtree
  and `rb_validate` will happily certify the (wrong) subtree as legal. Write a **stale-root
  regression test** the same day you write rotations.

**Deletion** — the unpleasant direction; damage is a *global count mismatch*, not a local violation.
- Removing a **red leaf** is free (no invariant impact).
- A node with **two children**: hoist the in-order successor's key+value into the doomed node's
  slot, then delete the successor instead (which has ≤1 child by construction). "Hoist" = transfer
  *ownership* of the key allocation — get this wrong and you get two nodes both believing they own
  the same key (→ double free at `rb_destroy` time).
- Every deletion funnels down to: **what happens when the physically unlinked node is black?**
  → creates a "doubly black" deficit — an **accounting fiction**, not a third color in the enum.
  The empty slot "owes" one black; fixup's job is paying that debt off by climbing toward the root.
- Deletion fixup case families (mirror images exist for all — don't forget them):
  - Sibling is black with no red children → recolor sibling red, debt moves up one level (if
    parent absorbs it by being red → turns black, done, no pointers moved — the "cheap" case,
    deletion's mirror of the red-uncle insert case).
  - Sibling has a red child → rotation drags that red across to the deficient side.
  - Sibling itself is red → rotate first just to reach a shape you already know how to handle.
  - Debt reaching the root just dissolves there (every path lost the same one black — equality
    restored, absolute black-height may drop by one, which is fine).
  - **Special/easy corner case:** deleting a black node with exactly one child. That child is
    *provably* red (proof by counting — a black child there would already have broken the tree
    before you touched it). Fix: splice the red child into the vacant slot, paint it black. Done —
    no debt, no fixup loop at all. **If your code launches the full sibling case analysis here,
    something is wrong** — this must be tested explicitly (spec calls out adding this exact case
    to the required table-driven tests).
- **Memory-safety tripwire repeated multiple times in the spec:** fixup must NEVER dereference
  freed memory. Either save everything you need (parent/sibling/slot info) *before* calling
  `free()` on the removed node, or restructure to free *after* fixup completes. Either order is
  fine; the ordering violation is not.

## From Java to C (field guide) — the two questions that matter for every pointer

For every pointer-like thing in this assignment, ask: **(1) how long does the pointee live, and
(2) who is responsible for eventually freeing it?** Java answered both silently; C answers neither.

- Pointer ≠ object. Copying a pointer copies an address, not the thing at that address (aliasing
  works like Java references — two names, one object — but *ownership* is a separate concept from
  *reachability*: many pointers can reach an object; exactly one owns it).
- `malloc(n)` gives raw, uninitialized, unconstructed bytes — nothing more. `free(p)` exactly once,
  never touch that pointer again after.
- Named failure modes: **leak** (never freed), **double free** (freed twice — corrupts allocator
  bookkeeping), **use-after-free** (freed then still used — "the most treacherous," because it
  often *keeps working* for a while).
- Local/stack variables die when their function returns — anything that must outlive the call
  (every tree node, every private key copy) needs heap storage via `malloc`.
- `malloc` **can return NULL** — must check every allocation. Partial-failure cleanup matters: if
  node alloc succeeds but the subsequent key-copy alloc fails, the first allocation is still yours
  to free ("the second malloc failed" is not an exemption from cleaning up the first).
- C strings are `char*` arrays terminated by `'\0'`. `==` on two strings compares **addresses**, not
  contents (bug you'll write once, remember forever) — use `strcmp(a,b) == 0`. Copying a string
  means `malloc(strlen(s) + 1)` — **never forget the +1** for the terminator.
- One logical tree node = **two separate heap allocations** (the node struct itself, and its private
  heap copy of the key string) — both must be tracked and freed, not just one.
- `struct` = fields only, no methods/constructors — `malloc`ing one gives raw bytes; you initialize
  every field yourself. Idiom: `malloc(sizeof *n)` — ties the allocation size to the pointer's type
  automatically.
- The public header uses an **opaque type** (`typedef struct rbtree rbtree_t;` with no visible
  fields) — C's version of "private," enforced by the compiler simply never being told the layout.
- A `parent` pointer is optional but common — makes fixup loops easier to write (classic textbook
  algorithms assume one), at the cost of one more pointer to keep correct through every rotation.
  **This is flagged as "your first real design decision."**

## Ownership contract (the actual grading contract — read like a lease)

- `rb_insert`: **on success**, the tree takes ownership of `value` (caller must never free it — the
  tree will, via `value_free`, when appropriate). **On failure** (`-1`), ownership never transferred
  — caller still owns `value` and must handle it. **On overwrite** of an existing key, the tree
  frees the *old* value before installing the new one (tree is the old value's only owner at that
  moment).
- Track three things separately per node: the node allocation, the tree's private key copy, and the
  opaque `value` (whose ownership follows the API rules above — not tied to node/key lifetime).
- Rotations change **topology only** — they never change who owns a node/key/value.

## Frozen API (`include/rbtree.h`) — NEVER MODIFY

```c
rbtree_t *rb_create(rb_value_free_fn value_free);      // NULL on alloc failure; value_free may be NULL
int       rb_insert(rbtree_t *t, const char *key, void *value); // 0 ok, -1 on alloc failure (unchanged, value NOT consumed)
void     *rb_find(const rbtree_t *t, const char *key);          // tree retains ownership
int       rb_delete(rbtree_t *t, const char *key);              // 0 ok, -1 if absent; frees key copy + value
size_t    rb_size(const rbtree_t *t);
void      rb_foreach(const rbtree_t *t, void (*fn)(const char*, void*, void*), void *ctx); // in-order
int       rb_validate(const rbtree_t *t);                       // 0 iff all invariants hold
void      rb_destroy(rbtree_t *t);                               // frees everything, NULL-safe
```
Keys are C strings, copied and owned by the tree. Values are opaque `void *`.

## Milestones (M0–M3 + optional Reach)

| Milestone | What | Est. hours |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Setup: repo, `CLAUDE.md`, toolchain | 1 |
| M1 | Skeleton, insert (+rebalance), find, foreach, validate | 3–4 |
| M2 | Delete (all fixup cases) + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops), green under asan+memcheck | 3–4 |
| M3 | Hardening, edge cases, final clean sweep | 1–2 |
| The Reach (ungraded) | Teardown *without recursion* — O(1) aux space via right-spine trick | 1–2 |
| — | Process artifacts (CLAUDE.md, PROMPTLOG.md, REFLECTION.md), written throughout | 1 |

**Discipline point emphasized repeatedly:** don't debug delete on top of an insert you don't trust
yet — "less a milestone than an archaeological dig."

### Required operations & testing bar
- Required: `rb_create`, `rb_insert` (w/ rebalancing), `rb_find`, `rb_delete` (full fixup, all
  cases), `rb_size`, `rb_foreach` (in-order), `rb_validate`, `rb_destroy`.
- `rb_validate` must check all 5 invariants + that `rb_size` matches actual node count.
- **Fuzzer:** ≥ 10⁵ random insert/find/delete ops vs. a reference model (sorted array or linked
  list is fine), calling `rb_validate` at least every 100 ops, under both asan and memcheck.
- **Targeted deletion tests are required in addition to fuzzing** (fuzzing alone won't reliably hit
  rare fixup shapes): minimum a red leaf, a black leaf with a red sibling, a two-children node,
  root deletion — **plus the black-node-with-one-red-child case** the spec adds explicitly. Each
  test must assert `rb_validate` and `rb_size` afterward.
- **Recursion is allowed** in `rb_destroy`/`rb_foreach` *for this assignment only* — the next
  assignment revokes it (stack-limited kernel-style constraints).
- **Tip explicitly recommended:** route all allocation through 4-line wrapper functions
  `rb_malloc`/`rb_free` (just forwarding to malloc/free for now) — this is the "seam" the *next*
  assignment's fault-injection harness will need. Install now, "while the house is small."

## Toolchain / verification requirements

- Must compile clean: `gcc -std=c23 -Wall -Wextra -Werror`.
- `make asan` — AddressSanitizer + UBSan (compiled-in instrumentation; fast, pinpoints the exact
  bad instruction).
- `make memcheck` — valgrind (external, no rebuild needed, catches some uninitialized-read cases
  ASan misses; much slower). Required together — "belt and suspenders," deliberately redundant.
- **Hard rule: a single leaked byte, invalid read/write, or UB report caps that milestone's
  correctness score at 50%.** Not a warning — a failure, mechanically enforced.

## Deliverables (submitted as a tar via Canvas)

- Source: Makefile, `src/rbtree.c`, tests, the **unmodified** frozen `include/rbtree.h`.
- `CLAUDE.md` — checked in, evolving across milestones.
- `PROMPTLOG.md` — **4–6 annotated episodes** (prompt + response + your judgment: accepted /
  rejected / pushed back, and why). Must include at minimum: one plan you revised, one
  rejected/oversized diff, one tool-output debugging loop, one review finding you triaged.
  **Raw transcript dumps score nothing here — annotation is the actual deliverable.**
- `REFLECTION.md` (~1 page): where the agent was most/least reliable; one bug it introduced that
  you caught and how; what most surprised "the Java programmer you were two weeks ago."
- **Raw Claude Code session transcripts** (`.jsonl` files, unmodified, not exported/retyped) —
  found locally at `~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl`. **These auto-purge after 30
  days** — copy them out periodically; losing them is not a valid excuse.
- Git history with **≥ 8 meaningful commits** tracking milestones — a single "final submission"
  commit is an **automatic process-grade of zero**.

## Grading breakdown (5 points total)

| Component | Method | Points |
|---|---|---|
| Core tree (insert/find/foreach/validate) | Unit tests + fuzzer (≥10⁵ ops) under asan+memcheck | 1.5 |
| Deletion, all fixup cases | Table-driven case tests + fuzzer w/ deletes green | 1.5 |
| Code quality & memory cleanliness | Clean build, zero sanitizer/valgrind findings, sane structure | 1.0 |
| **Program correctness subtotal** | | **4.0** |
| Prompt analysis (transcripts) | TA review for genuine iterative use, corroborated vs. repo | 0.5 |
| Quiz (live walkthrough, on your own code) | Short quiz generated from your submitted code | 0.5 |
| **Total** | | **5.0** |

### Transcript grading is evidence-based, not narrative-based
"The grade is based on what can be corroborated against the repository, never on the log's own
narrative." A grader (headless Claude) cross-checks claims in the transcript against actual git
commits/diffs/tests. **A confident but unverifiable story scores below a modest, checkable one.**
5-level scale, 0.1 pts per level: Level 5 = "verified engineering dialogue" (every episode
cross-checks against a commit/test/diff) down to Level 1 = "performative or contradicted" (narrative
conflicts with git history / episodes appear fabricated).

## Rules of engagement for AI use

- **Allowed/expected:** explore, plan, implement, test, debug, review with Claude Code; ask it to
  explain concepts; have it write test scaffolding/Makefiles.
- **Required:** the process deliverables above, raw transcripts, git history with ≥8 commits.
- **Forbidden:** submitting code you cannot personally explain. "Claude wrote it" is not an
  explanation.
- **You own the bugs.** If the agent introduces a use-after-free and you commit it, it's yours to
  explain, full stop.

## Personalized Verification (live walkthrough) — mandatory for EVERY student

Not a flagged-subset spot check — everyone sits for it. You'll be given a small, previously-unseen
modification to make live, starting only from your own submitted source (e.g. a new CLI flag, a
new key-length range). Plus questions about specific lines of your own code ("why is this node
recolored?", "what frees this key copy on the overwrite path?") and a `PROMPTLOG.md` episode you
must defend. **This is explicitly why understanding matters more than a working submission alone —
a static submission can only prove a plausible-looking result exists, not that you built it.**

## Workflow steps required (Section 11 of spec) — summarized (see howto-notes.md for the practical version)

1. Give the agent persistent context via `CLAUDE.md` (`/init` then hand-edit — build/test commands,
   frozen-header rule, style rules, "smallest change that passes").
2. Explore before writing anything (fresh session, questions only, no edits).
3. **Plan mode** (Shift+Tab) for every milestone — agent can read/analyze but not edit. Argue with
   the plan before approving; a plan accepted unmodified on first try is flagged as a red flag.
4. Tests first, then the smallest implementation slice — reject any diff that's too big ("one case
   only").
5. Close the loop with tool evidence — never accept "should pass now"; feed real tool output back.
6. Manage context: `/clear` between milestones, `/compact` mid-task when a debugging thread gets
   noisy. Rule of thumb: new milestone → new session.
7. **Adversarial review in a fresh context** before each milestone commit (`/code-review` skill or
   manually `/clear` + hostile-reviewer prompt) — hunts specifically for use-after-free in successor
   splice, leaked key copy on overwrite, unchecked NULL, missed subtrees in `rb_destroy`.
8. Git discipline — commit at every green state, conversationally directing the agent to do so
   *after you've read the diff*.
9. (Optional) Automate the battery as a slash command (`.claude/commands/battery.md`).

## Practical logistics

- Requires a **paid Claude subscription** ($20/mo Pro tier) — free tier won't carry this
  assignment. Two separate clocks: a **5-hour session window** (resets from first message) and a
  **weekly cap** (fixed reset day/time per account) — both shared across ALL Claude usage, not just
  this project.
- **Agent teams/parallel subagents should be left OFF** for this assignment — explicitly called out
  as a way to burn tokens without benefit ("buying the same wrong answer four times, concurrently").
- Suggested 2-week schedule: Week 1 = M0+M1 (setup through insertion green). Week 2 = M2+M3
  (deletion, fuzzing, hardening, process docs) + optional Reach + live walkthroughs.

## My standing takeaways for how I (Claude) should help on this assignment

- **Teach-first is not just my default here — it's structurally required by the grading.** A
  finished solution handed over defeats the actual point and would hurt Nick's grade (transcript
  analysis + live quiz + live code modification all specifically probe for genuine understanding).
- When we do start working, I should mirror the spec's own required workflow: explore → plan mode
  → argue the plan → smallest tested slice → verify with real tool output → adversarial review →
  commit. Not "here's the whole tree."
- Ownership tracking (node / key copy / value, as 3 separate things) is the single idea most likely
  to cause silent grading failures if fuzzy — worth being pedantic about every time we touch
  allocation or freeing.
- Nick should keep his own `PROMPTLOG.md`/`REFLECTION.md`/`DEVLOG.md` — these are graded artifacts
  and the value comes from *his* annotation/judgment, not from me writing them for him.

50	1 Overview
51	Everything in this assignment orbits a single data structure. A red-black tree is a small thing to
52	describe and a demanding thing to keep alive. Every node is a separately allocated heap object
53	stitched to its neighbors by pointers. Every insertion may allocate several times and then rebalance
54	by rewiring pointers far from the insertion point. Every deletion must repair global invariants while
55	releasing memory in exactly the right order. That combination makes the red-black tree an ideal
56	specimen for studying memory management, which is the part this course actually cares about.
57	You built the tree once, in Assignment 1. Here you keep it correct while the assignment re-
58	peatedly changes the rules about where its bytes live and how they may be reclaimed. By the end,
59	the logical tree is unchanged: same API, same invariants, same answers. Everything underneath it
60	has been replaced. If you finish with the sense that the balancing algorithm was the easy part, the
61	assignment has worked. The structure matters beyond the assignment’s perimeters, too. The Linux
62	kernel ships its own red-black tree library and leans on it wherever predictable O(log n) behavior
63	and tight memory control must coexist: most famously in the CFS scheduler’s runqueue (one of
64	the crown jewels of the CPU-scheduling module, where we will study it in depth) and, for several
65	years, in tracking the memory regions of every process’s address space.
66	The core theme here is discipline under a moving target. Writing a red-black tree that returns
67	the right answer is fairly straightforward, and you have already done it. Keeping that tree correct
68	when allocation can fail at an arbitrary point, when nodes must come from your own allocator,
69	when there is no stack to recurse on, and when two logical trees quietly share the same bytes: that
70	is the harder skill, and the one this assignment is actually grading. A tree that looks up the right
71	key but leaks, double-frees, or recurses unboundedly fails. Every correct answer it returns is beside
72	the point.

385	8 Part-1: The Mutations (Milestones 1–3)
386	Up to this point the tree has lived in the most forgiving world imaginable: every node it asked for,
387	it received, and every node it finished with, it was free to forget. That forgetting is the luxury this
388	part takes away. Three mutations follow, and not one of them changes what the tree computes; each
389	changes only the ground it stands on. To keep your footing you will need three ideas the baseline
390	never forced you to meet.
391	A useful way to read the next three milestones is as a sequence of increasingly strict contracts.
392	Mutation 1 says: memory allocation may fail. Mutation 2 says: nodes may no longer come from
393	the general-purpose allocator at all. Mutation 3 says: the call stack is no longer available as scratch
394	space for walking the tree. At each stage, the abstract data structure remains exactly the same.
395	Search still searches. Insert still inserts. The red-black invariants still hold. What keeps changing
396	is which implementation conveniences you are allowed to depend on.
397	That separation is an important systems idea in its own right. An abstraction tells callers what a
398	component does. Its implementation decides how resources are acquired, managed, and eventually
399	returned. Much of operating-systems work consists of changing the latter without allowing the
400	former to flinch.
401	The first is the memory leak. When you ask the allocator for a block, it hands you the bytes
402	and remembers nothing else about them; keeping track of that block is now entirely your problem.
403	Free it and it returns to circulation. Lose the last pointer to it without freeing, and the block is
404	stranded: still allocated, forever unreachable, dead weight until the process exits. In a program
405	that runs for a second, such a leak is a tree falling in an empty forest. In one that runs for months,
406	which is to say a kernel, a database, or a web server, leaks accumulate, and accumulation is fatal.
407	The cruelty is that they gather on precisely the paths you are least likely to test: the error paths,
408	where one allocation failed halfway through a chain of them, you returned early, and you quietly
409	forgot to release what you had already grabbed. Mutation 1 (Section 8.1) exists to walk down every
410	one of those paths and check. There is a second lesson hiding inside that one. Correctness under
411	failure is not merely “remember to free things.” Ideally, an operation should either complete or leave
412	the structure as though it had never started. You will encounter this idea again under other names:
413	failure atomicity, transactional behavior, commit points. Here you are learning it with two malloc
414	calls and a tree, which is a pleasantly small place to meet a very large idea.
415	The second idea is that asking for memory one node at a time is not free. Every call to malloc
416	must find a suitable block, record its size, align it, and stitch its own bookkeeping around it. Do that
417	a million times for a million identical little nodes and the bookkeeping starts to rival the payload!
418	While the nodes themselves scatter across the heap and your cache spends the day chasing pointers.

426	When every object is the same size, you can decline to play that game. Grab memory wholesale
427	in big page-sized chunks, slice each chunk into node-sized slots, and hand them out yourself; when
428	a node dies, thread its corpse onto a free list so the next request can reuse it without troubling
429	malloc at all. That is a pool allocator, and it turns both allocation and freeing into an O(1)
430	pointer shuffle. An analogy might be useful here. General-purpose malloc is a hotel desk that
431	handles guests needing rooms of every imaginable size and duration. Your pool has a much easier
432	job: every guest wants exactly the same room. Once you know that, you can build a corridor of
433	identical rooms and keep a list of which doors are available. There is much less deciding to do on
434	every arrival.
435	A related term you need for Mutation 2 is a slab. A slab is simply one of those wholesale chunks
436	from which many same-sized objects are carved. The allocator is the policy and machinery; the
